Senses.Explanation: The joined food words also name a monastery's scheduled communal meals and their provision. The Imperially Revised Baizhang Monastic Code, redacted by Dehui, schedules gruel and rice at two times and tea and hot water at three (二時上粥飯，三時上茶湯). Zhaozhou Congshen likewise says that, during his travels, the two scheduled gruel-and-rice meals were the only occasions that divided his attention (除二時粥飯是雜用心處). Baoning Renyong calls himself a gruel-and-rice host (粥飯主人) who receives travellers from north and south with salt, vinegar, sufficient gruel, and sufficient rice. Here the headword is not merely a list of two foods: it names recurring communal provision, its timetable, and the host responsible for it. Zen bends the ordinary food pair into the institutional vocabulary of monastery scheduling and hospitality.
Senses.Note: The allowlisted concordance has 668 hits in 223 texts. Institutional families include the two gruel-and-rice mealtimes (二時粥飯) and the gruel-and-rice host (粥飯主人). These are deployments of one communal meal system, not separate senses. That organized institution is distinct from the physical food eaten and smelled in the second sense.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Record of Ancestral Teaching Essentials (列祖提綱錄) preserves Baoning Renyong's account of becoming a gruel-and-rice host who receives travellers and maintains meal provision.

Senses.Explanation: Gruel and cooked rice are the physical foods smelled, tasted, eaten, and shown restoring movement in Chan records. This food referent is distinct from the monastery's organized meal schedule and provision. Shiwu Qinghong says that mountain-field gruel and rice smell fragrant (山田粥飯香). Foyan Qingyuan asks whether someone unfed gruel and rice for three days can move, then says that the person can move after eating some (不與粥飯喫三日……纔方喫得些粥飯方能動得). Boshan Wuyi says that only now, when eating gruel and rice, does he know sweetness (至今喫粥飯始知甜耳). Xueyan Zuqin describes residents merely following the crowd to eat gruel and rice and perform bodily functions (趂大隊，喫粥飯，屙屎送尿). Baichi Yuan's related enumeration places eating gruel and eating rice among ordinary bodily acts, while Tiebians Yunshao's rebuke derives a longer compound from consumed food, “puffing gruel-and-rice breath” (鼓粥飯氣). Eating, taste, fragrance, and restored movement predicate physical food, a different thing from the monastery's schedule and provision.
Senses.Note: Four exact headword witnesses establish the food referent through fragrance, nourishment, taste, and consumption. Two marked family witnesses preserve the separated eating formula and the food-derived breath compound without allowing either to count toward exact-headword depth. Longer compounds such as gruel-and-rice monk remain separate lexical families.
